To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) Online learning is faster, and can be as accurate as batch learning.
(1) online training is a good idea; (2) active learning is a good idea, too.

1) online learning is a practical alternative to batch learning; 2) online learning is faster than batch learning; 3) active example selection is a practical alternative for batch learning; 4) active example selection yields higher accuracy than random sampling; 5) active example selection can speed up learning; 6) active example selection reduces the number of examples needed for learning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of building fast kernel classifiers that can learn from very large training sets, and can be trained incrementally, without retraining from scratch when new examples are available.
learning algorithms that can handle large amounts of training data, while maintaining the accuracy of the learned model.
learning algorithms that are efficient in time and space, and that can be used in real world applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LASVM algorithm is a very fast and efficient learning algorithm that can yield very accurate models.
LASVM is a very good algorithm for large scale learning problems, and the active version of LASVM is a good choice when labels are expensive to acquire, or when the goal is to obtain a simple model.
LASVM is an extremely effective algorithm for learning in high-dimensional spaces, especially for problems where the training set is very large and/or the test set is very large.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, by combining online and active learning, we can train high-dimensional kernel classif iers with thousands of training examples in seconds.

, in the context of kernel classifiers, the cost of training can be reduced by orders of magnitude, while the performance is maintained or improved, by exploiting the availability of a large number of unlabeled examples.
we can now afford to train very high dimensional learning systems, with very large numbers of training examples, and still obtain very good results in a reasonable amount of time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cost of computing can be reduced by using a simple strategy to prioritize examples, which can be applied to a variety of learning algorithms.
, in high dimensional spaces, the best way to learn from examples is not necessarily to learn from all the examples.
